I ran one job on IQM's free Garnet test device, garnet:mock. The job ID is 01a160a6-4068-75b4-be0d-f10d30d1eef1. It held 6 circuits at times 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0, with 2000 shots each. It cost no credits.

How I built it: the 6 spins sit on a line of real Garnet qubits, QB1, QB2, QB5, QB4, QB3 and QB8, and neighbors in the chain are wired together on the chip. Each circuit first sets the pattern up, down, up, down, up, down. Then it applies the Heisenberg interaction J(SxSx + SySy + SzSz) on every neighbor pair, in small time steps of 0.25 or less (Trotter steps). The longest circuit, at t = 2, has 8 steps and 118 two-qubit CZ gates. I read the gate counts and the measured qubits back from the circuits the server stored.

What a perfect quantum computer would show for these circuits (Neel order, where 1 is the perfect up-down pattern):
t=0: 1.000, t=0.4: 0.882, t=0.8: 0.624, t=1.2: 0.415, t=1.6: 0.348, t=2.0: 0.380.
The exact Heisenberg answer without time steps is almost the same: 1.000, 0.882, 0.623, 0.411, 0.341, 0.371. This shows the time steps are small enough.

What the test device gave back: about -0.60 at every time (-0.601, -0.590, -0.599, -0.602, -0.599, -0.601). Even t=0 gives -0.60, and a circuit with only a few flips should give exactly 1 there. The test device does not run the circuit. It returns made-up bitstrings, always the same 8 patterns in about equal numbers, whatever the circuit is. These numbers only show that the job ran end to end. They say nothing about physics. A run on the real Garnet would cost credits and would also be hurt by noise from about 100 CZ gates.

What the physics shows: the perfect up-down pattern is not a stable state of the quantum Heisenberg model. The SxSx + SySy part of the interaction lets two neighboring opposite spins swap places. These swaps spread through the chain, so the order falls from 1 to about 0.35 by t = 1.6. After that it rises a little and wobbles, because the 6-spin chain is small and finite. In KCuF3 this effect is called quantum fluctuation. It is why the measured ordered moment of the copper spins is much smaller than a full classical up-down pattern would give. It is also why the chain behaves as a quantum liquid of spins down to low temperatures, and why neutron scattering sees a broad continuum of spinon excitations instead of sharp spin waves. A 6-spin simulation on short times only shows the start of this. It does not reproduce the material's measured numbers.
